short_description: Glucocorticoid Management Plan Documented (RA)
lay_term: The provider reports this code when he develops and documents a glucocorticoid management plan to monitor the length and dose of a glucocorticoid he uses to treat rheumatoid arthritis, or RA, in a patient. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation of the joints resulting in deformity, pain, and loss of function. This disease results in a hyperactive immune and inflammatory system that may affect the joints and other organs. The most common line of treatment that a provider follows to treat an RA patient is the use of glucocorticoid, or corticosteroids. These are substances that reduce inflammation; a provider may sometimes refer to them as a steroid. These medications are helpful in reducing the disease activity in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. A glucocorticoid management plan includes the documentation of the steroid prescription with the length of use, doses, and attempts of tapering the dosage of steroid to avoid dependency. The provider documents the glucocorticoid management plan and the date in the medical record for a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Terminology Autoimmune disorder: Response of the immune system against own body. Immune system: Body’s self defense mechanism that protects against disease. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Read Less

short_description: DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder documented at the initial evaluation (MDD, MDD ADOL)
lay_term: A provider uses this code to inform the payer of clinical decisions and to report quality measures to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) that helps in determining the quality of services. Explanation The provider uses this code when he treats a patient with a major depressive disorder, or MDD, at the initial evaluation to report the measure of quality. The provider’s documents should match the set of criteria for MDD in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM 5™. DSM 5™ clinical guidelines for MDD for example, may include such criteria as a depressed mood, significant weight loss or gain, fatigue or loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness, diminished ability to concentrate and recurrent thoughts of suicide. DSM 5™ then serves as a classification and diagnostic tool that providers universally use for psychiatric diagnoses and treatment recommendations. Terminology Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM 5™: The Fifth Edition of the manual, released in May 2013, by the American Psychiatric Association® (APA®). Tips The provider may also need to report an appropriate G code to indicate both documentation of the MDD criteria. Read Less

short_description: Functional status assessed (COA) (RA)
lay_term: The provider assesses the functional status of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, or RA. The assessment may evaluate the patient’s level of activities of daily living, or ADL, and or status of instrumental activities of daily living, or IADL. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation of the joints resulting in deformity, pain, and loss of function. This disease results in a hyperactive immune and inflammatory system that may affect the joints and other organs. The functional status is a measure of a patient’s ability to function normally and to carry out his daily activities. The provider uses different measurement concepts and tools to determine the functional status of the individual, for example, the index of independence in activities of daily living, provides a tool to detect problems in performing basic functions of daily living and to help plan care. A rapid disability rating scale assesses the level of a patient’s disability by a caregiver who summarizes the patient’s physical and mental functioning, and the physical self maintenance scale, gauges observable patient behaviors including ADL and IADL, or instrumental activities of daily living, which include such functions as the patient’s ability to manage finances, medications, and shopping. The provider documents the functional status result of the patient and the date of the assessment in the patient’s record. Terminology Activities of daily living (ADLs): Routine tasks that an individual performs every day without any assistance; includes the patient’s ability to perform certain functions such as bathing, dressing, toileting, continence, feeding, and transferring, or moving from bed to wheelchair, for example. Autoimmune disorder: Response of the immune system against own body. Index of independence in activities of daily living: An instrument to assess the functional status of the patient’s ability to perform activities of daily living. Instrumental activities of daily living, or IADL: Complex skills that an individual needs to successfully live independently; includes the patient’s ability to shop for groceries, drive, use of public transportation, use the telephone, prepare meals, do housework, home repair, laundry, take medications or handle finances. Immune system: Body’s self defense mechanism that protects against disease. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Physical self maintenance scale: A scale that provider uses to assess the self care and mobility in patients. Rapid disability rating scale: A scale that provider uses to measure the level of patient disability. Read Less

short_description: Neuropsychiatric symptoms assessed and results reviewed (DEM)
lay_term: The provider assesses the neuropsychiatric symptoms of a patient with dementia and reviews the results. The assessment may evaluate the disturbance in activity, mood, thought process, or perception of the patient. Explanation Dementia refers to a disorder of cognitive and functional impairment, characterized by difficulties with memory, learning, reasoning, personality changes, thinking, or other thought processes. The provider uses different measurement concepts and tools to determine the neuropsychiatric symptoms of the individual, which helps the provider to analyze the plan of care for the patient and assess the plans effectiveness. These tools include the dementia signs and symptoms scale or neuropsychiatric inventory. The neuropsychiatric inventory assesses such patient behavioral changes as to level of agitation, impulsiveness, aggressiveness, eating disturbances, sleep problems, irritability, anxiety, mood fluctuations, delusion, or hallucinations. The provider reports this code when he assesses both the neurological and psychiatric symptoms of a patient of any age with dementia and he reviews the results for the patient. He reports this code at least once within 12 month period. The provider documents the neuropsychiatric symptoms and test results for the patient, along with the date of the assessment in the patient’s healthcare record. Terminology Dementia signs and symptoms scale (DSSS): Assessment of features such as memory loss, impairment in judgement, loss of communication, balance problem, behavior changes, or others, as shown by a dementia patient. Neuropsychiatric: Pertains to the study of a diseases effect on the neurological, or nervous system, and the psychiatric, or mental or emotional, effect of the disorder. Read Less

short_description: Dilated retinal eye exam with interpretation by an ophthalmologist or optometrist documented and reviewed; without evidence of retinopathy (DM)
lay_term: The ophthalmology or optometry provider performs a dilated retinal eye exam in a diabetic patient with no evidence of diabetic retinopathy. He interprets the findings and documents them in the patient’s chart. Explanation The provider, an ophthalmologist or optometrist, instills dilating drops into the eye to dilate (widen) the pupil in a diabetic patient without evidence of retinopathy. Using a bright light and an ophthalmoscope, he examines the back of the eye, focusing on the retina and optic nerve for signs of damage or disease. Terminology Diabetes mellitus (DM): A disease in which the body's production or utilization of insulin, the primary hormone involved in glucose metabolism, is insufficient, leading to high levels of blood glucose and subsequent complications, including significant damage to nerves, vessels, and multiple organs; type 1 DM refers to insulin–dependent diabetes mellitus; type 2 DM refers to a form that can be controlled with oral or injectable noninsulin medications. Ophthalmologist: A licensed medical doctor (MD) or osteopathic physician (DO), who provides vision testing and care and who can prescribe topical and systemic medicines and perform surgery. Ophthalmoscopy: Examination of the internal surfaces of the hollow eye cavity through a dilated pupil; in indirect ophthalmoscopy the machine produces an inverted image of the fundus of the eye. Optometrist: A Doctor of Optometry (DO) who performs eye exams and vision tests, prescribes and dispenses corrective lenses (glasses or contact lenses), detects certain eye abnormalities, and can prescribe topical medications; optometrists cannot perform eye surgery. Retina: Tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. Retinopathy: Damage to the blood vessels feeding the light–sensitive tissue at the back of the eye (the retina), which results in impaired vision; a common cause of retinopathy is diabetes. Tips For dilated retinal eye exam in diabetic patients with evidence of retinopathy, see 2022F. Additional Info Category II codes are tracking codes for performance measurement. These codes are used for data collection and to reflect quality of care; they correspond to nationally established performance measures. These codes are not used for reimbursement, and their reporting is optional. They cannot be used in place of Category I codes for procedures and services. Read Less

lay_term: A trained nonphysician genetic counselor analyzes a patient’s family risk factors for genetic conditions, analyzes available medical information, and counsels the patient and, possibly, family. This code represents each 30 minutes of total time the genetic counselor provides on the encounter date. Explanation A trained nonphysician genetic counselor collects information about the patient’s genetic health, which may include reviewing medical records and interviewing family members, to get a structured family genetic history. The provider may coordinate tests for the patient. The provider uses the information to create a family pedigree to assist with assessing genetic risks for the patient, who may or may not currently be exhibiting signs or symptoms of disease. The provider creates a formal report including analysis and any recommendations. The provider also counsels the patient and, possibly, family to help them understand the findings, management options, genetic risk within the family, and other related areas including the emotions that surround diagnosis. This code represents each 30 minutes of total time the genetic counselor provides on the encounter date. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline These services are provided by trained genetic counselors and may include obtaining a structured family genetic history, pedigree construction, analysis for genetic risk assessment, and counseling of the patient and family. short_description: Colorectal cancer screening results documented and reviewed (PV)
lay_term: Colorectal cancer screening includes radiologic, endoscopic, and laboratory tests to assess the colon, or lower part of the large intestine, and the rectum for cancer in individuals at age 50 or older. The code includes the interpretation of the results of the procedure by the provider and its documentation. Unlike diagnostic tests, there do not need to be signs, symptoms, or history of colon disease in order to cover a screening exam. Explanation The provider performs an annual laboratory test of the patient’s stool to detect hidden blood, known as fecal occult blood testing or a guaiac test. Every five years, the provider also performs a flexible sigmoidoscopy, which is an examination of the sigmoid colon, which is the lower part of the colon, and the rectum, using an endoscope inserted in the rectum, or he may perform a double contrast barium enema, a radiologic exam in which X–rays are taken of the lower intestinal tract after the patient ingests barium, a contrast medium, and the provider injects air in the colon to provide additional contrast and helping to illuminate the colon on X–ray films. Alternatively, every ten years, the provider may perform a colonoscopy, an examination of the entire colon using an endoscope inserted in the rectum. During these examinations, the provider inspects the lower intestine for evidence of an abnormal mass, or tumor, such as an adenoma, a benign glandular tumor, or a neoplasm, a cancerous tumor. Medicare policies cover this service for beneficiaries of 50 years of age or older. It also covers a beneficiary at high risk for colorectal cancer without regard to age every two years. Otherwise the beneficiary is liable for payment. Early detection with subsequent removal of adenomas and other neoplasms that may develop into cancer help to lower cancer rates. The provider evaluates the screening results and documents the findings in it. The provider documents the presence of an adenoma or other neoplasm and the date of the test in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) less than 40% or documentation of moderately or severely depressed left ventricular systolic function (CAD, HF)
lay_term: A provider reports this code when a patient’s condition is such that his left ventricular ejection fraction or, LVEF, is less than 40 percent or when his left ventricular systolic function, or LVS function, is moderately or severely depressed. Explanation Left ventricular ejection fraction is the measurement of the amount of blood that the left ventricle of a patient’s heart pumps out with each contraction. A left ventricular ejection fraction or, LVEF, less than 40 percent is an indication of heart failure when the heart muscle weakens and the heart does not contract effectively. Left ventricular systolic function, or LVS function, is a measure of how well the left ventricle of the heart contracts and sends blood to the rest of the body. A moderately or severely depressed left ventricular systolic function is also an indication of heart failure. The provider most commonly uses an echocardiogram to determine the left ventricular ejection fraction or left ventricular systolic function. The provider documents in the patient’s medical record that the patient has a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 40 percent or the patient has a moderately or severely depressed left ventricular systolic function. Ejection fraction (EF): The measure of percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with every heartbeat. Heart failure: A state in which a patient’s heart is not able to pump blood sufficiently to meet the needs of the body. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): The measurement of the amount of blood that the left ventricle of the heart pumps out with each contraction. Ventricle of the heart: One of four chambers in the human heart; two upper auricles or atria, and two lower ventricles; auricles supply blood to the ventricles and the ventricles pump blood to the organs of the body through blood vessels called arteries. Section Specific Guideline The following section of Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) contains a set of supplemental tracking codes that can be used for performance measurement. It is anticipated that the use of Category II codes for performance measurement will decrease the need for record abstraction and chart review, and thereby minimize administrative burden on physicians, other health care professionals, hospitals, and entities seeking to measure the quality of patient care. These codes are intended to facilitate data collection about the quality of care rendered by coding certain services and test results that support nationally established performance measures and that have an evidence base as contributing to quality patient care. The use of these codes is optional. The codes are not required for correct coding and may not be used as a substitute for Category I codes. These codes describe clinical components that may be typically included in evaluation and management services or clinical services and, therefore, do not have a relative value associated with them. Category II codes may also describe results from clinical laboratory or radiology tests and other procedures, identified processes intended to address patient safety practices, or services reflecting compliance with state or federal law. Category II codes described in this section make use of alphabetical characters as the 5th character in the string (ie, 4 digits followed by the letter F). These digits are not intended to reflect the placement of the code in the regular (Category I) part of the CPT® code set. To promote understanding of these codes and their associated measures, users are referred to the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing, which contains information about performance measurement exclusion modifiers, measures, and the measure's source. Cross-references to the measures associated with each Category II code and their source are included for reference in the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing. In addition, acronyms for the related diseases or clinical condition(s) have been added at the end of each code descriptor to identify the topic or clinical category in which that code is included. A complete listing of the diseases/clinical conditions, and their acronyms are provided in alphabetical order in the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing. The Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing can be accessed on the website at https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/cpt/category-ii-codes. Users should review the complete measure(s) associated with each code prior to implementation. Requests for Category II CPT® codes will be reviewed by the CPT/HCPAC Advisory Committee just as requests for Category I CPT® codes are reviewed. short_description: Estrogen receptor (ER) or progesterone receptor (PR) positive breast cancer (ONC)
lay_term: The provider assesses the presence of estrogen or progesterone receptors, cell proteins that bind to specific molecules, within tumor cells in female patients, 18 years of age or older. A tumor that is estrogen or progesterone receptor positive (ER+ or PR+) responds to medications that interfere with the production or utilization of estrogen. Explanation Estrogen and progesterone are female hormones essential for the growth of certain breast cancer cells. If breast cancer tissue contains estrogen or progesterone receptors, these hormones may enter the tumor and enhance its growth. The provider assesses the presence of estrogen or progesterone receptors in patients with invasive breast cancer or a reoccurrence of cancer. The treatment of a patient depends upon the presence or absence of these receptors. A provider prescribes tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors for ER+ or PR+ breast cancer because these medications interfere with the production or utilization of estrogen in the body and prevent cancer growth. The provider reports this code in a female patient, 18 years of age or older, who is positive for breast cancer in which the tumor contains estrogen or progesterone receptors. The provider documents the presence of ER+ or PR+ breast cancer and the date of the test in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: AJCC Breast Cancer Stage I: T1c (tumor size > 1 cm to 2 cm) documented (ONC)
lay_term: The provider diagnoses a female patient, 18 years of age or older, with breast cancer and documents it as stage I, with a subclassification of T1c, wherein the size of the tumor is greater than 1 cm but less than or equal to 2cm in its greatest dimension. Explanation The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) classifies cancer at a particular site according to the size of the primary tumor, expressed as T; involvement of regional lymph nodes, expressed as N; and the presence of distant metastases, or spread of cancer, expressed as N. The AJCC divides stage I breast cancers into stage IA and stage IB. Stage IA cancers are stated to be T1N0M0, with T1 broken down into T1mic, T1a, T1b, and T1c. Stage IB cancers are stated to be either T0N1miM0 or T1N1miM0, in which N1mi stands for microscopic, or extremely small, lymph node invasion. The body produces female hormones estrogen and progesterone, which are essential for the growth of certain breast cancers, said to be estrogen or progesterone receptor positive (ER+ or PR+). A provider prescribes tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors because they interfere with the production or utilization of estrogen in the body and prevent cancer growth. The provider reports this code to document either stage IA or IB breast cancer, subclassified as T1c, in female patients, 18 years of age or older. T1c designates a tumor larger than 1 cm but less than or equal to 2 cm in greatest dimension. He records the code at least once within a year for patients with progesterone or estrogen receptor positive tumors and who are prescribed tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor. The provider documents the stage of breast cancer and the date of the measurement in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: AJCC Breast Cancer Stage IV documented (ONC)
lay_term: The provider diagnoses a female patient, 18 years of age or older, with breast cancer and documents it as stage IV, wherein the size of the tumor may be of any dimension and distant metastases, or spread of the cancer, is present. M1 indicates distant metastases demonstrated clinically, radiographically, or histologically, i.e., examination of tissue under a microscope. The body produces female hormones estrogen and progesterone, which are essential for the growth of certain breast cancers, said to be estrogen or progesterone receptor positive, or ER+ or PR+. A provider prescribes tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors because they interfere with the production or utilization of estrogen in the body and prevent cancer growth. The provider reports this code to document stage IV breast cancer in female patients, 18 years of age or older. He records the code at least once within a year. short_description: AJCC colon cancer, Stage 0 documented (ONC)

short_description: AJCC colon cancer, Stage II documented (ONC)
lay_term: The provider diagnoses a patient, 18 years of age or older, with colon cancer and documents it as stage II, wherein the tumor invades the deepest layers of the colon, from the muscularis propria into the pericolorectal tissues. It may reach the visceral peritoneum (inside of the membrane lining the abdomen) and adhere to or invade other organs or structures. Explanation The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) classifies cancer at a particular site according to the size of the primary tumor, expressed as T; involvement of regional lymph nodes, expressed as N; and the presence of any distant metastases (spread of cancer), expressed as M. Stage IIA cancers are stated to be T3N0M0, in which T3 represents invasion of tumor through the muscularis propria into the pericolorectal tissues. Stage IIB cancers are stated to be T4aN0M0, in which T4a represents tumor penetration into the surface of the membrane lining the abdomen (visceral peritoneum). Stage IIC cancers are stated to be T4bN0M0, in which T4b represents tumor invasion or adherence to other organs or structures. There is no nodal involvement and no distant metastases. For later stage colon cancer, the provider may prescribe adjuvant chemotherapy (cancer drugs given following surgery or other primary treatment). The provider reports this code to document stages IIA, IIB, and IIC colon cancer in patients 18 years of age or older. He records the code at least once within a year. The provider documents the stage of colon cancer and the date of the measurement in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: AJCC colon cancer, Stage III documented (ONC)
lay_term: The provider diagnoses a patient, 18 years of age or older, with colon cancer and documents it as stage III, which means the tumor invades any layer of the colon, may attack other organs or structures, and includes regional lymph node involvement. Explanation The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) classifies cancer at a particular site according to the size of the primary tumor, expressed as T; involvement of lymph nodes, expressed as N; and the presence of distant metastases (spread of cancer), expressed as M. The AJCC divides stage III colon cancers into stages IIIA, IIIB, and IIIC. Stage IIIA cancers are stated to be T1 or T2 with N1 or N1c, and M0 or T1N2aM0. Stage IIIB cancers are stated to be T3 or T4a with N1 or N1c, and M0; T2 or T3 with N2aM0; or T1 orT2 with N2bM0. Stage IIIC cancers are stated to be T4aN2aM0; T3 or T4a with N2bM0; or T4b with N1 or N2, and M0. Size of the primary tumor is expressed as T, where T1 represents submucosal layer invasion, just below the surface; T2 represents invasion of the muscularis propria, one of the inner layers of the colon; T3 represents invasion that goes through muscularis propria and into the pericolorectal tissues, the deepest layer; T4a represents penetration of the inner membrane lining of the abdomen (visceral peritoneum); and T4b represents tumor invasion or adherence to other organs or structures. Lymph node involvement is expressed as N, where N refers to metastases (spread of cancer) to one to three regional lymph nodes, with N1a indicating one node and N1b two to three nodes. N1c represents cancerous cells in specific tissues, including the subserosal layer, mesentery, nonperitonealized pericolonic, or perirectal tissues, but without regional lymph node metastasis. N2 represents metastases in four or more regional lymph nodes, with N2a indicating four to six nodes and N2b seven or more nodes. In stage III cancers, there are no distant metastases. The provider may prescribe adjuvant chemotherapy (cancer drugs administered following surgery or other primary treatment). The provider reports this code to document stage III colon cancer in patients 18 years of age or older. He records the code at least once within a year. The provider documents the stage of colon cancer and the date of the measurement in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: AJCC colon cancer, Stage IV documented (ONC)
lay_term: The provider diagnoses a patient, 18 years of age or older, with colon cancer and documents it as stage IV, wherein the tumor invades any layer of the colon, involves regional lymph nodes, and includes distant metastases (spread of cancer) to other organs or structures. Explanation The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) classifies cancer at a particular site according to the size of the primary tumor, expressed as T; involvement of lymph nodes, expressed as N; and the presence of distant metastases, expressed as M. The AJCC divides stage IV colon cancer into stages IVA and IVB. Stage IVA cancers are stated to be any T, any N, and M1a, in which metastasis is confined to a single organ or site. Stage IVB cancers are stated to be any T, any N, and M1b, in which metastases involves more than one organ and or site or includes the peritoneum (lining of the abdominal cavity). The provider may prescribe adjuvant chemotherapy (cancer drugs given following surgery or other primary treatment). The provider reports this code to document the stage IV of colon cancer in patients of 18 years of age or older. He records the code at least once within a year. The provider documents the stage of colon cancer and the date of the measurement in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: TB screening performed and results interpreted within six months prior to initiation of first-time biologic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drug therapy for RA (RA)
lay_term: Rheumatoid arthritis patients who are on disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy are at a higher risk for reactivation of a latent tuberculosis infection. Latent tuberculosis means that the patient is infected with the tuberculosis bacteria (TB) however, the patient does not have active tuberculosis. The provider screens the rheumatoid arthritis patient for TB before starting a disease–modifying antirheumatic drug therapy. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic disease that causes disabling inflammation in a patient's joints. This disease results in hyperactive immune and inflammatory systems that may affect the joints and other organs. Disease–modifying antirheumatic drugs are a group of medications that the provider uses in patients with rheumatoid arthritis to decrease pain and inflammation by suppressing the body’s overactive immune and inflammatory system. The use of the antirheumatic drug may reactivate a latent tuberculosis infection in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. The provider screens the patient for tuberculosis through a skin TB test before initiating the drug therapy regimen. He then performs and interprets the result of the TB test. He usually performs a screening six months prior to initiation of first time disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy. Whenever the provider screens the patient for TB before initiating a disease–modifying antirheumatic drug therapy, he documents the date of the test in the patient's medical record. Read Less

short_description: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) disease activity, low (RA)
lay_term: The rheumatoid arthritis disease activity score determines the disease activity level of a patient, which helps assess the degree of inflammation and the patient’s level of pain due to rheumatoid arthritis. The provider may adjust the patient’s rheumatoid arthritis medication depending on the results of the score. The provider reports this code when a patient has a low RA score. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis, or RA, is an autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation of the joints resulting in deformity, pain, and loss of function. This disease results in a hyperactive immune and inflammatory system that may affect the joints and other organs. The Disease Activity Score or, DAS is a combined outcome of measure that evaluates the number of joints that are swollen or tender, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, ESR, or C reactive protein, CRP in the blood to measure the degree of inflammation and the VAS or, Visual Analogue Score to determine the level of pain. The outcome of these parameters gives a score that correlates with the extent of the disease activity. A disease Activity Score between 2.6 and 3.2 signifies a low disease activity. The provider documents the disease activity score and the date of the test in the patient’s record. Terminology Autoimmune disorder: Response of the immune system against own body. C reactive protein or, CRP: A blood test that measures the level of protein called C reactive protein in the blood, which determines the level of inflammation in the body. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, or ESR: A nonspecific blood test for inflammation that can be an indicator of neoplastic diseases, autoimmune disorders, and infection. Immune system: Body’s self defense mechanism that protects against disease. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. VAS or, Visual Analogue Score: An instrument of measure that measures the pain intensity on a scale of 0 to 10. Read Less

short_description: Disease prognosis for rheumatoid arthritis assessed, poor prognosis documented (RA)
lay_term: The provider assesses the disease prognosis, or the future progression of a disease in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis to determine the severity and persistence of the disease activity. The provider reports this code when the patient has a poor prognosis. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation of the joints resulting in deformity, pain, and loss of function. This disease results in a hyperactive immune and inflammatory system that may affect the joints and other organs. The symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis can change from day to day. The provider evaluates the patient periodically to determine the prognosis of the disease on the basis of the progression of the disease and level of bony damage due to inflammation. He uses tools such as functional status measurement tools, to measure a patient’s ability to function normally and to carry out daily activities of living and disease activity scores to determine the level of disease progression. Use this code for quality reporting purposes when the provider basis his assessment of the patient documents the poor prognosis of the disease. Functional status: It is a measure of ability of the individual to function normally and to carry out his daily activities. Immune system: Body’s self defense mechanism that protects against disease. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Prognosis: Likely outcome or course of the disease. Read Less

short_description: Statin therapy prescribed or currently being taken (CAD)
lay_term: A provider uses this code to report that the provider prescribes or the patient is currently taking a statin therapy. Statins are drugs that lower the level of cholesterol in blood as it reduces its production in liver. The provider may adjust the patient’s statin therapy depending on his condition. Explanation The provider prescribes or the patient is currently taking a statin therapy. Statins are drug that lowers the level of cholesterol in the patient’s blood by reducing its production in the liver. Statins block the enzyme in the liver that is responsible for making cholesterol. An increase in a patient’s cholesterol level may lead to development of plaque inside the blood vessels, known as atherosclerosis. This leads to a restricted flow of blood through the blood vessels that supply blood to the heart, which in turn hampers the proper functioning of the heart, causing conditions such as chest pain (angina) and coronary artery disease (CAD). Statins not only reduce the production of cholesterol, but they also reduce the formation of new plaques and occasionally can reduce the size of plaques that already exist. The provider documents a statin therapy prescription and the date of the treatment in the patient’s record. Terminology Cholesterol: An important fatlike substance found in most tissues; an important component in certain processes but excessive accumulation can cause atherosclerosis and circulation problems. Coronary artery disease or CAD: A condition in which the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle become stenosed due to the deposit of plaques or fatty substances on the inner walls of the blood vessels, resulting in decreased blood flow and ultimately heart failure, if not treated; also known as coronary heart disease or atherosclerotic heart disease. Enzymes: Biological compounds that act as selective catalysts to increase the rate and specificity of certain biochemical reactions, such as breaking down a specific compound. Plaque: Yellowish deposits of cholesterol and other lipid material, that is, fat, in the lining (intima) of the arteries. Read Less

short_description: Pneumococcal vaccine administered or previously received (COPD) (PV) (IBD)
lay_term: Pneumococcal vaccine triggers the immune response of the patient and protects against infection from pneumococcus bacteria, an infectious organism. The provider administers the vaccine to all children younger than five years of age and all adults who are older than 65 years. He also administers the vaccine to individuals of six through 64 years of age with certain medical conditions, like asthma, which is a lung condition. He reports this code either when the individual receives the vaccine, or if the individual received the vaccine previously. Explanation Pneumococcus bacterium causes a group of diseases, or pneumococcal diseases, which include pneumonia, a severe lung condition; bacterial meningitis, an inflammation of the covering of the brain and spinal cord; and sinus tract infections, which involve the sinuses cavities connected to the nasal passages. Children younger than five years of age and adults who are older than 65 years of age have greater risk for life threatening complications from these diseases, so the provider vaccinates these individuals against pneumococcus. He administers pneumococcal vaccine through the intramuscular route. Medicare policies cover this service for their beneficiaries. Sometimes the individual receives the immunization from another provider or from the same provider during another reporting period. Under such circumstances, the provider should report whether the individual has been given an immunization or not. The provider documents the administration of pneumococcal vaccine and the date of the immunization in the patient’s healthcare record. Read Less

short_description: Internal mammary artery graft performed for primary, isolated coronary artery bypass graft procedure (CABG)
lay_term: When there is narrowing, stiffness, or blockage of the coronary arteries and the patient has symptoms such as chest pain, the provider tests the patient and confirms a clinical diagnosis of heart disease. The provider then performs a coronary artery bypass graft surgery using an internal mammary graft to treat the condition and relieve the chest pain and other symptoms. An internal mammary artery graft, also known as an internal thoracic artery graft, is the most common graft taken from the chest area of a patient for a coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG procedure. Explanation When the patient complains of chest pain, the provider orders certain tests to confirm heart disease. Once the test reports confirm the patient has coronary artery disease, which is a build up of fat, cholesterol, and calcium deposits on the walls of the arteries that narrow the arteries of the heart and reduce the blood supply to the heart muscle, the provider performs coronary artery bypass graft surgery using an internal mammary artery graft. The provider harvests a healthy internal mammary artery from the patient’s chest and grafts them into the coronary arteries to allow blood flow to bypass a blockage. Providers prefer an internal mammary artery graft because of its patency. The provider documents the use of the internal mammary artery graft for the primary isolated coronary artery bypass graft, CABG, surgery in the patient’s record. Terminology Coronary artery bypass graft: Placing a vein graft between the aorta and one or more of the obstructed main arteries of the heart to reestablish blood flow to the portion of the heart served by that artery; providers sometimes anastomose, or join, the coronary artery to a mammary or other artery instead of the aorta. Coronary artery: One of the major arteries that supplies blood to the ventricle and atrium of the heart. Internal mammary artery, internal thoracic artery: The artery supplying the thoracic, or chest, wall, mediastinum, the organs and structures in the chest, and diaphragm, the membrane dividing the abdominal and chest cavities; sometimes used for bypass in coronary artery bypass graft surgery. These codes describe clinical components that may be typically included in evaluation and management services or clinical services and, therefore, do not have a relative value associated with them. Category II codes may also describe results from clinical laboratory or radiology tests and other procedures, identified processes intended to address patient safety practices, or services reflecting compliance with state or federal law. Category II codes described in this section make use of alphabetical characters as the 5th character in the string (ie, 4 digits followed by the letter F). These digits are not intended to reflect the placement of the code in the regular (Category I) part of the CPT® code set. To promote understanding of these codes and their associated measures, users are referred to the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing, which contains information about performance measurement exclusion modifiers, measures, and the measure's source. Cross-references to the measures associated with each Category II code and their source are included for reference in the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing. short_description: Disease modifying anti-rheumatic drug therapy prescribed or dispensed (RA)
lay_term: The provider reports this code to indicate that he prescribes or dispenses a disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy to a patient. Disease modifying antirheumatic drugs are a group of medications that the provider uses for patients with rheumatoid arthritis to decrease pain and inflammation by suppressing the body’s overactive immune and inflammatory system. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic disease that causes disabling inflammation in the joints. This disease results in hyperactive immune and inflammatory systems that may affect the joints and other organs. Disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy may take several weeks or months to ease pain and inflammation. The provider closely monitors the therapy as these drugs can be toxic. He has the patient undergo lab tests to make sure that use of the anti rheumatic drug is not affecting the patient’s liver, kidney, and blood. Depending upon the benefit of the therapy the provider may prescribe one or more medication for life time use in some patients. Whenever the provider prescribes, dispenses, or administers antirheumatic drug therapy, he documents this in the patient's medical record, along with the date. Terminology Autoimmune disorder: Disease caused by the reaction of antibodies against own body proteins. Immune system: Body’s self defense mechanism that protects against disease. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Read Less

short_description: Patient receiving first-time biologic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drug therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
lay_term: The provider uses this code to report that he prescribes a disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy for the first time to a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Disease modifying antirheumatic drugs are a group of medications that the provider uses in patients with rheumatoid arthritis to decrease pain and inflammation by suppressing the body’s overactive immune and inflammatory systems. Explanation Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic disease that causes disabling inflammation in a patient's joints. This disease results in hyperactive immune and inflammatory systems that may affect the joints and other organs. Disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy may take several weeks or months to ease pain and inflammation. The provider closely monitors the therapy as these drugs can be toxic. He has the patient undergo some lab tests to make sure that use of the antirheumatic drug is not affecting the patient’s liver, kidney, and blood. Depending upon the benefit of the therapy the provider may prescribe one or more medications for life time use in some patients. Whenever the provider prescribes an antirheumatic drug therapy for the first time to any patient, he documents this in the patient's medical reccord along with the date. Terminology Autoimmune disorder: Disease caused by the reaction of antibodies against own body proteins. Immune system: Body’s self defense mechanism that protects against disease. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Read Less

short_description: Patient (or caregiver) queried about sleep disturbances (Prkns)
lay_term: The provider inquires about a Parkinson’s patients sleep disorders in order to plan treatment efficiently. Parkinson’s disease is a form of a progressive nervous system disorder, which has tremors as the main characteristic. Patients also suffer from stiffness, disturbed posture, and sleep abnormalities during the course of the disease. Explanation Parkinson’s disease is a movement disorder. It is a form of a progressive nervous system disorder, which has tremors as the main characteristic. Patients suffer from stiffness and a disturbed posture, which makes the patient unable to carry out any movement smoothly. The provider queries the patient or their caregiver about any sleep disturbances the patient may be experiencing during the course of the disease, which mainly occurs as a result of disturbed motor functions. The patient might suffer daytime sleepiness, sleep attacks, sleep apnea, or breath disturbances, during sleep. The provider also inquires about such sleep disturbances as tremors or stiffness at night, frequent urination, or nightmares. Sometimes, Parkinsons medication can cause an increase in a patient's day time sleepiness as well. A good night sleep is important for a Parkinson’s patient and the provider advices the patient about good sleep arrangements, which includes establishing a good sleep pattern, and having a comfortable bed with an optimal room temperature. He may also recommend exercising regularly as it can also help alleviate the patient’s sleep disorders. The provider documents the results of his sleep related inquiries and the date of encounter in the patient’s record. Obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA: Condition occurring during sleep in which breathing stops intermittently for brief periods, disrupting the sleep cycle and resulting in daytime sleepiness, due to obstruction, narrowing, or incompetence of the airway. short_description: Rehabilitative therapy options discussed with patient (or caregiver) (Prkns)
lay_term: The provider discusses the rehabilitation therapy options that a patient with Parkinson’s disease has to reduce or overcome the effects of the disorder. Parkinson’s disease is a form of a progressive nervous system disorder, which has tremors as the main characteristic. Patients also suffer from stiffness, disturbed posture, and sleep abnormalities during the course of the disease. Explanation Parkinson’s disease is a movement disorder. It is a form of a progressive nervous system disorder, which has tremors as the main characteristic. Patients suffer from stiffness and a disturbed posture, which makes the patient unable to carry out any movement smoothly. Apart from the movement disorders, the patient also suffers from behavioural disorders, with depression being the most common. There is also slowing of the speech and as the disease progresses, the symptoms worsen. Apart from the medications the provider prescribes, rehabilitation plays an important role in improving the function and the quality of life of a Parkinson’s patient. The provider discusses the rehabilitation options with the patient or the caregiver. Therapy involves a large amount of attention to improving the gait or the walking pattern of the individual. Improving the patient’s balance and flexibility, and initiating a movement are also important. Rehabilitation also works to modify the patient’s daily living activities so that the patient can perform daily tasks, like eating, more easily. Along with the above movement services, speech and language therapy is given to the patient. The provider documents the results of discussions of the importance of rehabilitation and the date of encounter in the patient’s record. Terminology Parkinson’s disease: A progressive movement disorder of the nervous system that h is mainly characterised by postural instability, tremors, and sleep disturbances. Rehabilitation: Form of treatment to improve the normal functions. Read Less

It is anticipated that the use of Category II codes for performance measurement will decrease the need for record abstraction and chart review, and thereby minimize administrative burden on physicians, other health care professionals, hospitals, and entities seeking to measure the quality of patient care. These codes are intended to facilitate data collection about the quality of care rendered by coding certain services and test results that support nationally established performance measures and that have an evidence base as contributing to quality patient care. The use of these codes is optional. The codes are not required for correct coding and may not be used as a substitute for Category I codes. These codes describe clinical components that may be typically included in evaluation and management services or clinical services and, therefore, do not have a relative value associated with them. Category II codes may also describe results from clinical laboratory or radiology tests and other procedures, identified processes intended to address patient safety practices, or services reflecting compliance with state or federal law. Category II codes described in this section make use of alphabetical characters as the 5th character in the string (ie, 4 digits followed by the letter F). These digits are not intended to reflect the placement of the code in the regular (Category I) part of the CPT® code set. To promote understanding of these codes and their associated measures, users are referred to the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing, which contains information about performance measurement exclusion modifiers, measures, and the measure's source. Cross-references to the measures associated with each Category II code and their source are included for reference in the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing. In addition, acronyms for the related diseases or clinical condition(s) have been added at the end of each code descriptor to identify the topic or clinical category in which that code is included. A complete listing of the diseases/clinical conditions, and their acronyms are provided in alphabetical order in the Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing. The Alphabetical Clinical Topics Listing can be accessed on the website at https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/cpt/category-ii-codes. Users should review the complete measure(s) associated with each code prior to implementation. Requests for Category II CPT® codes will be reviewed by the CPT/HCPAC Advisory Committee just as requests for Category I CPT® codes are reviewed. These codes describe clinical components that may be typically included in evaluation and management services or clinical services and, therefore, do not have a relative value associated with them. short_description: Other carotid stenosis: Ipsilateral TIA or stroke 120 days or greater prior to procedure or any prior contralateral carotid territory or vertebrobasilar TIA or stroke (NMA-No Measure Associated)
lay_term: The provider documents that a patient has a type of carotid artery stenosis evidenced by an ipsilateral transient ischemic attack or stroke 120 or more days prior to a surgical procedure or a prior contralateral TIA or stroke originating in the arteries of the neck or base of the brain. Explanation The carotid arteries are a pair of major arteries that carry oxygen–rich blood to the brain. The vertebrobasilar arteries run through the neck into the base of the brain. Sticky deposits, known as plaques, can build up on the artery walls, narrowing these passages and increasing the risk of blockage, which can cause stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), which are interruptions in blood flow that starve the brain of oxygen. Reporting this code indicates the patient had a same–side (ipsilateral) carotid territory TIA or stroke 120 days or more before the procedure being reported, or the patient had any prior opposite side (contralateral) carotid or vertebrobasilar TIA or stroke. There is currently no measure associated with this code. Read Less

In developing new and revised performance measurement codes, requests for codes are considered from: measurements that were developed and tested by a national organization; evidenced-based measurements with established ties to health outcomes; measurements that address clinical conditions of high prevalence, high risk, or high cost; and well-established measurements that are currently being used by large segments of the health care industry across the country.
